method: For a near-Gaussian analog resolution filter the sweep time is the constant k times the span divided by the resolution bandwidth squared, so narrowing the RBW by ten multiplies the sweep time by a hundred. The span is the stop frequency minus the start frequency, both taken in the chosen unit; the sweep rate is the span divided by the sweep time, which equals the RBW squared divided by k; the resolution elements across the span are the span divided by the RBW. A k of 2 to 3 covers the Gaussian filters swept analyzers were built around, so a rate above RBW squared over 2 (k below 2) is reported as faster than the filter can settle, a rate from RBW squared over 3 to RBW squared over 2 as typical, and a slower rate as waiting longer than needed. With an optional time budget the widest usable RBW is the square root of k times the span divided by the budget, the resolution elements at that RBW are the span divided by it, and the rate at that RBW is the span divided by the budget; an RBW wider than the 1 GHz cap is reported with a note. Span, RBW, rates and resolution elements are rounded to 12 significant digits and the sweep time and its ten-times neighbours likewise. Start and stop frequencies from 0 to 1 THz with the stop above the start, an RBW above 0 and at most 1 GHz, k from 1 to 10 and an optional budget above 0 and at most 1000000 s are accepted. Text, exponent notation, a blank required field, an unknown unit and a value outside those ranges are refused with the exact reason, and decimal commas are accepted. This is the formula for a swept analog analyzer: it does not model a particular instrument's sweep-time limit, its FFT, oversweep or error-correction modes, or its errors at a given rate. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Keysight, Optimizing Spectrum Analyzer Measurement Speed (application note 5968-3411): for near-Gaussian analog resolution filters the sweep time is k times the span divided by the RBW squared, and a ten times narrower RBW multiplies the sweep time by a hundred.

UC Santa Barbara ECE 145A, Spectrum Analyzer notes: the filter rise time is K over the RBW with K = 2 to 3 for a Gaussian filter, so the sweep time is K times the span over the RBW squared, and sweeping faster than that leaves the response uncalibrated.
